text: From the SanMitra Newsroom,
this is the Daily AI Brief for 12 November 2026.
First, today's top headlines:
Rights groups urge a treaty on "killer robots" before
next week's UN talks.
Google launches the Gemini Decisions API for fast yes/no
and scoring calls.
DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 predicts how DNA changes affect
individual cell types.
Baidu launches ERNIE Lightning and a video model at
Baidu World 2026.
Japan weighs binding orders and penalties for AI firms
after incidents.
OpenAI now processes API requests inside India.
Databricks launches an always-on Genie agent for
enterprise work.
United Airlines restricts third-party AI agents from
booking flights.
Google releases A2UI 1.0,
an open standard for AI-generated screens.
Beijing plans capacity for 200,000 robots a year by
And now, the news in brief.
Our lead story today.
Three advocacy organisations want governments to start
negotiating a binding legal protocol on autonomous
weapons, with a firm deadline,
when states meet in Geneva next week.
Human Rights Watch says it is making the call together
with Amnesty International and the Stop Killer Robots
campaign ahead of the Convention on Conventional Weapons
Review Conference, which is scheduled for 16 to 20
November.
The conference meets just once in five years,
so the groups see it as an unusual opportunity.
They say weapons that can choose and strike targets
without meaningful human control are already being
tested and used.
Many countries support a binding treaty.
Leading military powers, however,
have preferred voluntary guidelines,
and discussions under the convention have been stuck for
over ten years.
Turning to the United States.
Google has unveiled Gemini Decision 1 along with a new
Decisions API.
The system is built to give quick verdicts rather than
long written responses.
In a single pass,
the model can work through as many as 1,000 closed
questions about one input.
Those can be yes-or-no questions,
multiple choice, or scoring against a rubric.
Inputs can be text,
images, audio, video or PDF files.
Google says results come back with probabilities and
confidence scores within 150 to 250 milliseconds.
The price is ten cents per million input tokens,
and output is free.
The company is aiming it at tasks inside AI agents,
such as routing requests,
checking policies and grading work,
where speed counts for more than a lengthy answer.
In other news.
Google DeepMind has announced AlphaGenome 2,
a model that forecasts how differences in DNA affect
various human cell types.
It was trained on over 100 million single-cell profiles
drawn from 68 tissues.
DeepMind says that, compared with its earlier model,
it spots close to twice as many variants that alter gene
expression in particular cell types.
A single genetic variant can behave differently
depending on which cell carries it,
so predictions at the level of individual cells could
help scientists work out how diseases develop.
Researchers doing non-commercial work can use it through
the AlphaGenome API, and commercial research has access
through a private preview.
The model is meant for research and is not approved for
clinical diagnosis.
In China.
Baidu used its Baidu World 2026 conference to unveil two
new models, according to TPS Report.
ERNIE Lightning is a reasoning model designed primarily
for Baidu Search.
ERNIE-Wizshot-ME turns a single photograph into a
talking video with expressive faces and costs 0.7 yuan
for each second of footage.
Business customers can use both through Baidu's Qianfan
cloud platform.
Baidu claims Lightning lowers the cost of its inference
engine, the system that runs its models,
by over 30 percent on chips from Kunlunxin,
Baidu's in-house chip unit.
That figure comes from Baidu,
which has released no benchmarks.
The launches show Baidu's drive to power its AI with
domestic chips while US export controls restrict access
to Nvidia hardware.
In Asia.
Kyodo News reports, citing a .
A government working group is examining the country's
2025 AI law, which relies on voluntary cooperation and
carries no penalties of any kind.
An outline of the review is expected by the end of the
year.
Such a step would be a change of direction for Japan.
Among major economies, it has so far taken one of the
lightest approaches to regulating AI.
The review comes amid rising concern about the misuse of
powerful models and about cyber incidents linked to AI.
Turning to India.
OpenAI has begun processing API requests locally in
India, The Week reports.
For supported workloads, both the incoming request and
the model's computation now take place within the
country, which goes further than just storing data
there.
The service starts with GPT-6 Luna through the Responses
and Chat Completions APIs.
Supported customer content is also kept in India.
The offering targets businesses that face rules
requiring data to stay in the country,
including banks and other financial companies.
For regulated organisations, where data is processed can
be as important as where it is stored.
The change could therefore remove a significant barrier
to using AI in sensitive business workflows.
Turning to the United States.
Databricks has unveiled the latest generation of its
Genie AI agent.
It is designed to keep working on complex business tasks
around the clock instead of simply answering questions
from staff.
The company says Genie can watch over data,
handle longer assignments and bring findings to people
without being prompted.
A business ontology, essentially a structured map of the
company, gives it context about an organisation's data,
staff and processes.
For administrators, Databricks describes several
controls.
These include restricting which tools the agent may use,
keeping a record of each action it takes and capping its
spending.
The launch is part of a broader move away from
assistants that wait for instructions and toward agents
that work as operational coworkers,
with governance designed in from the outset.
Next.
United Airlines says it is limiting outside AI agents
from using its website and app to make bookings and
other changes for customers.
The airline points to risks involving account
credentials, purchases customers never meant to make,
and changes to reservations and loyalty points.
It also cites rules that require a person to give
certain acknowledgements, for example confirming baggage
restrictions when checking in.
The decision draws a practical line for agentic AI.
Even if an agent is capable of booking a flight,
a company will not necessarily let it make purchases for
a customer.
Before agents can shop for people,
businesses will need clear policies on identity,
authorisation, liability and human sign-off.
Elsewhere.
Google has announced version 1.0 of A2UI,
an open protocol that lets AI agents respond with
interactive screens rather than plain text.
The agent describes an interface,
such as a form or a chart,
and the app then builds it from its own native
components.
The result matches the look and feel of the rest of the
app.
The new version adds function calls that work in both
directions, along with renderers for web and mobile
frameworks.
Instead of reading a wall of text and then doing the
next step manually, users could be shown a screen to
check, adjust and approve.
Because the standard is open,
agents and apps from other companies can use it as well.
In China.
Beijing's industry bureau has released an action plan
for embodied AI, meaning AI that runs physical machines
such as robots, covering 2026 to 2028,
EastFrontier reports.
The plan calls for a minimum of five world-class
humanoid robot manufacturers and no fewer than 200
robot-related firms.
It also sets a goal of being able to produce 200,000
robots annually, and of a 50,000-petaflop computing
cluster for training robot AI models.
The plan is dated 11 November.
China is betting big on humanoid and service robots as
an emerging industry, and city governments are competing
to attract the top manufacturers.
Beijing is already home to several humanoid start-ups
and held the first humanoid robot games.
The plan aims to move from prototypes to mass
production.
From the research desk.
The researchers behind a paper titled Scaling
Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks
are tackling a weakness in how AI language models learn
mathematics.
Training material is usually chopped into isolated
problems with answers.
That loses the order of topics and the links between
ideas found in the original books.
In response, the researchers built TOME-Math.
They drew it from 2,118 university-level textbooks and
turned those into about 380 thousand proof records.
The collection keeps chapters in sequence,
pairs each statement with its proof,
follows references between results and logs where every
entry came from.
After full training on this data,
the model's average test score rose 16.7 percentage
points above the base model,
and it also beat three public training datasets.
To recap today's top stories.
Rights groups urge a treaty on "killer robots" before
next week's UN talks.
Google launches the Gemini Decisions API for fast yes/no
and scoring calls.
DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 predicts how DNA changes affect
individual cell types.
Baidu launches ERNIE Lightning and a video model at
Baidu World 2026.
Japan weighs binding orders and penalties for AI firms
after incidents.
OpenAI now processes API requests inside India.
Those were today's critical developments across global
artificial intelligence.
From our bureaus covering World,
USA, China, Asia, and India,
thank you for watching SanMitra AI News Wire.
